code.source:
def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        print("Liftoff")
        return
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)
countdown(3)

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: a missing base case
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Our countdown has no base case. It prints three, two, one, zero, minus one, and keeps going. After about a thousand calls, Python stops it with a recursion error, maximum recursion depth exceeded. Python protects itself from endless calls. Add a base case that returns, and the countdown ends.

shorts.title: What is recursion?
shorts.script: Recursion means a function calls itself. Each call works on a smaller version of the problem. Think of Russian dolls. Open one, and you find a smaller doll, until you reach the smallest, which does not open. That smallest one is the base case, and it stops the whole process. Recursion is natural for problems that contain smaller copies of themselves. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Dolls inside dolls.

shorts.title: The base case
shorts.hook: "Every recursive function needs a base case."
shorts.script: Every recursive function needs a base case. It is the simplest version of the problem, which the function answers directly, without calling itself. For factorial, factorial of one is one. Without it, the function calls itself forever. Always write the base case first, then write the call that makes the problem smaller. Check that it really gets smaller. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Write it first.

shorts.title: Calls wait
shorts.hook: "Here is how factorial of five works."
shorts.script: Here is how factorial of five works. It calls factorial of four, and waits. That calls factorial of three, and waits. Down to factorial of one, which answers one. Then the waiting calls finish, one by one, multiplying on the way back. Two, six, twenty four, one hundred twenty. Each call keeps its own copy of n. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Calls wait for answers.

shorts.title: Recursion error
shorts.hook: "What if you forget the base case?"
shorts.script: What if you forget the base case? The function keeps calling itself, with smaller and smaller numbers, and never stops. After about a thousand calls, Python protects itself, and raises a recursion error, maximum recursion depth exceeded. The fix is a base case that returns. Whenever you see this error, ask, what stops this function? Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Add a base case.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "To understand recursion, you must first understand recursion."
shorts.script: To understand recursion, you must first understand recursion. Your challenge. Write a recursive function called total, that adds one plus two, up to n. The base case is n equals one, which returns one. Otherwise return n plus total of n minus one. Print total of four. You should see ten. Share your function below. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
